strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: learning reusable scene-level representations directly from 3D Gaussian splats, rather than only attaching task-specific semantic features or focusing on rendering. This is a useful direction for 3D scene understanding.

The multi-teacher design is technically plausible and well motivated. Distilling language-aligned, general visual, and object-aware teachers into a shared 3DGS encoder is a natural extension of prior lift-and-align work, and the per-teacher projectors plus standardization make the approach reasonably coherent.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The manuscript reports zero-shot semantic segmentation across ScanNet200, Matterport3D, ScanNet++, and InteriorGS; open-vocabulary instance segmentation; VQA integration; probing/finetuning on point-cloud tasks; data-efficiency experiments; adaptation cost; runtime; and several ablations.

The reported results are generally strong. Chorus improves over SceneSplat on 3DGS zero-shot segmentation, is competitive or better than strong point-cloud pretraining baselines in probing/finetuning, and shows especially good performance on fine-grained ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ settings.

The render-and-distill adaptation idea is practically useful. Avoiding large precomputed 3D teacher-feature storage while retaining performance gains is a meaningful systems contribution, even if the core idea is conceptually simple.
The ablations support some key design choices: adding DINO and PE improves zero-shot segmentation, 3DGS-aware augmentations and SmoothL1 help, and staged PE training appears beneficial.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than high. The work builds heavily on SceneSplat-style 2D-to-3D feature lifting and on known multi-teacher distillation; the main contribution is a strong combination and scaling of these ingredients for 3DGS rather than a fundamentally new representation-learning principle.

Some major claims are broader than the direct evidence. The paper calls the encoder holistic and general-purpose, but the strongest ablations are mostly on semantic segmentation. The contribution of each teacher to instance segmentation, VQA, and point-cloud transfer is less directly isolated.

The comparison setup is complicated and not always fully transparent from the main paper. Methods differ in modality, training sources, number of scenes, availability of 2D inputs, and pretraining objectives. The tables partially indicate this, but the fairness of several comparisons depends on details relegated to the supplement or not fully specified.

The point-cloud transfer result is interesting but under-explained. The proposed explanation via noise robustness is supported only by a small retrieval experiment on 10 ScanNet++ validation scenes and scaling curves; this does not fully establish why the 3DGS-pretrained variant transfers so well to conventional point clouds.

The VQA evidence is relatively weak compared with the strength of the claim. Improvements are small, one ScanQA metric decreases relative to the SceneSplat-based GaussianVLM baseline, and the evaluation mainly shows that Chorus can substitute as a backbone rather than demonstrating a substantially new reasoning capability.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript. Several important details are deferred to the supplement, including contrastive-loss equations, augmentation formulas, and view sampling details; code and models are only promised after publication. The use of newly processed pseudo-labels and a 3DGS-native InteriorGS benchmark also requires clear release and split details to be reproducible.

There are some presentation and consistency issues: for example, the text reports a ScanNet++ finetuning value that does not appear to match Table 4, and several tables use dense notation and mixed symbols that make the experimental protocol harder to parse. These are not fatal but reduce confidence and clarity.

strengths: The problem is timely: learning transferable scene representations directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives is relevant, and a native 3DGS encoder with multi-teacher distillation could be useful for downstream 3D scene understanding.

The evaluation attempts to cover many tasks, including open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, probing/finetuning, data-efficient supervision, VQA, and point-cloud transfer, rather than reporting only one narrow benchmark.

The reported numbers suggest some genuine empirical gains over SceneSplat and point-cloud baselines in several settings, especially ScanNet200/ScanNet++ probing and some open-vocabulary semantic segmentation results.
The render-and-distill adaptation idea is practically motivated and the paper gives a useful resource comparison against offline uplifting, suggesting a path to reduce storage/preprocessing burden.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an assembly of existing ingredients: lifted 2D teacher features, multi-teacher distillation, per-teacher projection heads, contrastive losses, and a Sonata-style backbone. The paper does not make a strong case that the method is conceptually novel beyond combining strong recent 2D teachers for 3DGS.

The evidence for the strongest claims is not fully convincing. Many gains are modest or mixed: in VQA, Chorus improves some metrics but ScanQA METEOR is lower than the SceneSplat variant, contradicting the claim of consistent improvement; in open-vocabulary instance segmentation, head-class mAP is worse than Mosaic3D despite better tail performance.

Comparisons are potentially unfair or under-explained. Chorus benefits from very strong 2D foundation teachers and pseudo-label processing, yet the paper emphasizes using fewer training scenes than point-cloud pretraining baselines without adequately accounting for teacher pretraining data, pseudo-label generation cost, compute, or differences in modality and supervision.

Reproducibility is weak in the provided manuscript. Several important details are deferred to the supplement, including augmentation equations, contrastive-loss details, view-pairing specifics, training schedules, and hyperparameters. Code and models are only promised upon publication.

The point-cloud transfer claim is surprising but insufficiently isolated. The paper does not clearly disentangle benefits from 3DGS-derived data, multi-teacher pseudo-labels, backbone choice, teacher strength, or data distribution. The robustness analysis uses only 10 ScanNet++ validation scenes and 684 instances, which is too limited to support broad conclusions.

The 3DGS-aware augmentation contribution is under-specified in the main paper and supported mainly by an aggregate ablation figure. Without equations or quantitative per-component tables in the manuscript, it is difficult to assess technical correctness or reproduce the effect.

The new InteriorGS-native benchmark is used as an important evaluation target, but dataset construction, label quality, splits, and possible overlap or domain relationship with training data are not described enough to judge whether the benchmark supports the claims.

Some writing and presentation issues affect trust in the results: there are inconsistent statements such as the text claiming 50.2 mIoU on ScanNet++ while Table 4 reports 52.9, overstatements such as “state-of-the-art across a broad spectrum,” and repeated reliance on “supplement” for material needed to evaluate the method.

Overall, the paper has worthwhile empirical ambitions, but the balance currently favors rejection because the novelty is incremental, several headline claims are overstated, and the experimental protocol/reproducibility details are not strong enough to support acceptance at CVPR.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely gap: learning reusable scene-level representations directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives rather than only attaching task-specific semantic fields or relying on point-cloud encoders. The multi-teacher formulation is well motivated, combining language-aligned, general visual, and object-aware 2D teachers into a shared 3DGS encoder with lightweight projectors.

The empirical scope is unusually broad and supports the central claim of versatility. Chorus is evaluated on zero-shot semantic segmentation across ScanNet200, Matterport3D, ScanNet++, and InteriorGS; open-vocabulary instance segmentation; VQA/grounding through GaussianVLM; probing and finetuning for semantic and instance segmentation; data-efficient learning; and teacher/design ablations.

The results are strong in several settings. For example, in zero-shot semantic segmentation Chorus improves over SceneSplat on ScanNet200 and InteriorGS, and the point-cloud-compatible variant gives large linear-probing gains over Sonata on ScanNet200 and ScanNet++. The instance segmentation and data-efficiency results further suggest that the learned representation is not narrowly tuned to one benchmark.

The render-and-distill adaptation idea is practical and useful. The reported comparison against precomputed uplifting supervision is compelling, reducing storage from about 1080 GB to 8 GB on InteriorGS while still improving downstream probing performance after adaptation.

The paper includes meaningful analysis beyond headline numbers, including teacher ablations, design-choice ablations, runtime/model-size reporting, scaling behavior, and a robustness-style retrieval test from point clouds to perturbed point clouds.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental at the conceptual level: the method largely extends lift-then-align 3DGS pretraining with multiple 2D teachers, PHI-S-style standardization, and task-specific heads. This is a reasonable and useful combination, but the core ingredients are mostly inherited from recent 2D/3D distillation and SceneSplat-style pipelines.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The VQA claim of consistent improvement is slightly overstated because ScanQA METEOR decreases compared with the SceneSplat GaussianVLM baseline, even though other metrics improve. Similarly, the data-efficiency discussion should distinguish finetuning, where Chorus is consistently better, from linear/decoder probing, where Chorus is worse than Sonata in some low-data settings such as 1% and 5% training scenes.

The fairness and interpretation of comparisons need care. Chorus uses powerful and very recent 2D teachers, newly processed pseudo-labels, and 3DGS-derived pretraining; comparisons to point-cloud SSL methods such as Sonata are interesting but not fully apples-to-apples. The paper would benefit from a clearer accounting of teacher compute, preprocessing cost, and whether baselines could gain similarly from stronger teacher supervision.

Reproducibility is only partially supported in the manuscript. Several important details are deferred to the supplement, including contrastive-loss equations, augmentation equations, view-pairing details, and additional training settings, while code and models are only promised upon publication. This makes independent reproduction difficult from the main paper alone.

The newly proposed InteriorGS-native benchmark is useful, but the manuscript provides limited detail in the main text about its label quality, splits, annotation protocol, and possible overlap or bias relative to pretraining data. Since several claims use InteriorGS to demonstrate 3DGS-native generalization and adaptation, this benchmark needs stronger documentation.

Ablations support the multi-teacher design, but the main paper does not fully isolate all teacher contributions. The table fixes the language teacher and adds DINO/PE; the claimed non-redundancy of every teacher would be more convincing with full combinations, especially removing SigLIP from the main results rather than only deferring it to the supplement.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant gap: learning reusable scene-level features directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives rather than only attaching task-specific semantic fields. The framing of 3DGS as a pretraining substrate is useful for CV/3D perception.

The multi-teacher design is technically sensible. Distilling SigLIP2, DINOv3, and PE-Spatial through a shared 3D encoder with teacher-specific heads is a natural way to combine language alignment, general visual structure, and object-aware locality.

The experimental coverage is unusually broad: open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary instance segmentation, probing/finetuning, data-efficient settings, VQA/grounding, robustness to 3DGS optimization/density, and cross-modality point-cloud transfer.

The reported results are generally strong. Chorus improves over SceneSplat on zero-shot 3DGS semantic segmentation, improves tail-class open-vocabulary instance segmentation, and gives notable gains over Sonata in several probing and finetuning settings, especially ScanNet200 and ScanNet++.

The ablations support several design choices: adding DINO and PE improves over language-only supervision, 3DGS-aware augmentations and contrastive terms add incremental gains, and rendering-based adaptation appears to reduce storage/preprocessing cost while improving InteriorGS performance.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to SceneSplat/lift-then-align pipelines: the main conceptual change is multi-teacher distillation plus additional evaluation breadth. This is valuable, but the paper sometimes presents the contribution as more foundational than the methodological novelty alone supports.

Several comparisons are not perfectly clean. Chorus benefits from large 2D foundation teachers, offline pseudo-label lifting, and 3DGS reconstructions, while some point-cloud baselines have different training signals, data sources, and modalities. The paper reports scene-count efficiency, but does not fully account for teacher compute, feature extraction cost, or reconstruction/pseudo-label generation cost.

Some headline claims are stronger than the numbers justify. Absolute zero-shot mIoU values remain modest, some metrics are mixed or small in magnitude, and the VQA gains are not uniformly positive on every metric. For example, ScanQA METEOR slightly decreases while ROUGE improves.

The point-cloud transfer result is interesting but not fully explained. The hypothesis that 3DGS pretraining acts as augmentation is supported by retrieval and visualization, but the distribution gap between optimized Gaussian centers/colors/normals and real point clouds remains under-analyzed.

The rendering-based adaptation pipeline is promising, but parts of the supplement suggest dependence on scene-specific information such as labeled points for height selection in pose sampling. This weakens the impression that adaptation is fully lightweight and annotation-free in all settings.

Reproducibility is only moderately convincing. The supplement gives many useful details, but the manuscript still relies on substantial custom data processing, updated Matterport3D 3DGS generation, teacher pseudo-label pipelines, and a placeholder-style code release statement. Exact end-to-end reproduction would likely be difficult without released scripts and processed data.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: learning feed-forward scene representations directly from 3D Gaussian splats, rather than only attaching task-specific features to a reconstructed scene. This is a useful direction for 3D scene understanding.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The paper reports open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary instance segmentation, semantic and instance probing/finetuning, low-data settings, VQA transfer, robustness to 3DGS optimization variants, and adaptation experiments across ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and InteriorGS.

The main quantitative results are generally strong. Chorus improves over SceneSplat on zero-shot 3DGS semantic segmentation, e.g. 24.6 vs. 22.5 f-mIoU on ScanNet200 and 15.7 vs. 10.0 f-mIoU on InteriorGS under joint training, and shows clear gains over Sonata on several point-cloud probing and finetuning settings.

The ablations support several design choices: adding DINO and PE-Spatial improves over the language-only teacher, 3DGS-aware augmentations and contrastive terms provide incremental gains, and the method appears reasonably robust to alternate 3DGS optimization/density and iPhone RGB-D point clouds.

The render-and-distill adaptation idea is practically useful, reducing storage from roughly 1080 GB to 8 GB in the reported InteriorGS setting while still improving linear probing performance after adaptation.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. The core recipe is a fairly direct extension of SceneSplat-style lift-and-align distillation with multiple 2D teachers, teacher-specific heads, and standard regression/contrastive losses. The paper sells this as a holistic encoder, but much of the contribution is careful system integration and evaluation rather than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The paper repeatedly suggests state-of-the-art or broad superiority, but results are mixed in places: Chorus is not always better than Sonata in decoder probing or instance segmentation on ScanNet, VQA gains are small on ScanQA, and 3D+2D methods still outperform Chorus substantially for open-vocabulary instance segmentation.

The point-cloud comparison is not entirely clean. Chorus benefits from strong 2D foundation teacher supervision and 3DGS-derived pretraining, while Sonata is a different self-supervised point-cloud method. The paper argues data efficiency using fewer scenes, but it does not fully normalize for teacher compute, pseudo-label generation cost, modality differences, or dataset/source differences.

The new InteriorGS benchmark construction introduces possible label noise and evaluation bias. Gaussian labels are assigned from bounding boxes using connected components, but the paper does not provide validation of label quality, human inspection statistics, or sensitivity analysis showing that conclusions are stable under this heuristic.

The adaptation results are promising but limited. The main reported gain is a +2.7 mIoU linear-probing improvement on InteriorGS, while broader downstream effects on the paper's main open-vocabulary, instance, or VQA tasks are not convincingly established.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Important implementation choices are scattered across main/supplement, some figures contain qualitative or plot-only results without exact numbers, and the paper says code is released at “this repository” but the manuscript text does not provide a concrete link. The dependence on large offline teacher feature extraction also makes reproduction costly.

The writing occasionally overstates the contribution and has minor polish issues, including awkward grammar such as “our codebase are released,” inconsistent notation/formatting, and dense tables whose comparison conditions are easy to miss. These are presentation issues, but they amplify the concern that some comparisons are less clean than presented.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important gap: learning transferable scene features directly from 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives rather than only attaching task-specific features for rendering or open-vocabulary segmentation.

The method is technically plausible and cleanly formulated: a shared 3DGS encoder with teacher-specific projection heads, standardized teacher features, matching losses, optional semantic/instance contrastive terms, 3DGS-aware augmentations, and a render-and-distill adaptation route.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this area, covering zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary instance segmentation, semantic and instance probing/finetuning, data-efficient training, VQA/grounding, robustness to 3DGS variants, and point-cloud transfer.

The reported gains over the closest 3DGS baseline, SceneSplat, are meaningful on several core metrics: for example, joint-data zero-shot semantic segmentation improves from 22.5 to 24.6 f-mIoU on ScanNet200 and from 10.0 to 15.7 f-mIoU on InteriorGS, with consistent gains on ScanNet++ and Matterport3D.

The point-cloud transfer result is a strong and interesting finding. Despite being pretrained from Gaussian-derived data, the point-cloud variant outperforms Sonata on several linear probing and finetuning settings, especially ScanNet200 and ScanNet++, suggesting the multi-teacher signals are not merely overfitting to 3DGS-specific parameters.

The ablations support the central design choices: adding DINO and PE-Spatial improves zero-shot performance over the language teacher alone, and the paper provides additional analyses for teacher resolution, pretraining scale, input perturbation robustness, 3DGS density, and optimization variants.
The proposed render-and-distill adaptation is practically useful, reducing precomputed feature storage substantially compared with offline uplifting and showing an InteriorGS adaptation gain.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than radical. The work extends a lift-then-align distillation paradigm from SceneSplat with multiple 2D teachers and broader evaluation; this is valuable, but many components are inherited from existing 2D teacher distillation, 3DGS feature lifting, and Sonata-style encoders.

Some claims are broader than the strongest evidence supports. The paper repeatedly frames Chorus as a holistic general-purpose encoder, but the improvements are uneven: VQA gains are small on ScanQA EM1/METEOR, instance segmentation still depends on Mask3D proposals, and in open-vocabulary instance segmentation methods using 3D+2D inputs remain substantially stronger.

The data-efficiency story is not uniformly favorable. In Table 5, Chorus is stronger after full finetuning, but linear and decoder probing under very limited scenes are mixed or worse than Sonata at 1% and 5%, so the claim should be scoped more carefully.

The new InteriorGS benchmark is useful but introduces uncertainty: labels are assigned from boxes to Gaussians via connected-component heuristics, and the paper does not provide enough validation of label quality or annotation noise. Since several important generalization and adaptation claims rely on InteriorGS, this matters.

The render-and-distill adaptation evidence is still limited. It is mainly demonstrated on InteriorGS with figures/ablations rather than a wide set of out-of-domain datasets, so its generality remains less established than the main pretraining results.

Fairness and reproducibility are mostly addressed but not perfect. The authors retrain SceneSplat due to their updated Matterport3D processing, and some baselines are taken from prior work while others use official checkpoints. The manuscript says the code is released at a repository, but the provided version does not make the release details concrete.

The method is computationally and systemically complex: it depends on multiple large 2D foundation teachers, feature uplifting, PHI-S preprocessing, optional label-based contrastive terms, and 3DGS-specific preprocessing. This does not undermine the result, but it raises the barrier to independent reproduction and deployment.

Several presentation issues slightly obscure the evidence, including dense tables, occasional formatting/extraction problems, and a few overstatements such as implying state-of-the-art performance across broad task families when some comparisons are conditional on input modality or proposal source.
